platforms.title: Shin Pain Isn't Just Muscle Soreness — Here's the Truth
platforms.meta_description: Aching pain along the inner shin after running isn't ordinary soreness — it's often shin splints. Mayo Clinic explains why and how it differs from a fracture.
platforms.body_html:
Started running or suddenly bumped up your mileage, and now the inside of your shin aches with every step? It's tempting to write it off as ordinary muscle soreness that'll fade in a day or two, but Mayo Clinic identifies this pattern as shin splints (medial tibial stress syndrome). Unlike garden-variety soreness, it's a real injury — repeated impact building up damage in the bone and surrounding tissue — that can get worse without the right management.

Why the inner shin hurts first

The periosteum (the membrane covering your shinbone) and the muscles and tendons attached to it absorb repeated impact every time your foot strikes the ground while running. When mileage or intensity increases suddenly, that tissue doesn't get time to adapt to the new load, and small damage accumulates — that buildup is the real mechanism behind shin splints. The bone itself hasn't fractured; it's inflammation in the periosteum and soft tissue, which is why the pain typically spreads along several inches of the inner edge of the shinbone rather than sitting in one spot.

Certain factors clearly raise the risk. Running on hard concrete or slanted surfaces, wearing worn-out or under-cushioned shoes, and having flat feet or high arches that lead to overpronation are among the biggest contributors. Add training hard without warming up, or running every single day without rest, and the tissue never gets a chance to recover, so symptoms show up much faster.

How to tell it apart from a stress fracture

Shin splints are easy to confuse with a stress fracture, but the distinction matters. Shin splints cause diffuse pain spread along the inner edge of the shinbone that gradually eases once you stop running. A stress fracture, on the other hand, produces sharp, pinpoint pain at one exact spot when pressed, and it often doesn't settle with rest — sometimes it even hurts just to walk. This distinction matters because shin splints can be managed by adjusting activity, while running through an undiagnosed stress fracture can progress into an actual break.

First, back off high-impact activity for a few days and switch to swimming or cycling instead. The goal isn't total rest — it's reducing the amount of impact your shin absorbs.

Second, ice the area after activity and use a foam roller on your calves. Tight calf muscles keep pulling on the shinbone and slow recovery, and loosening them regularly eases that load.

Third, sports medicine guidelines suggest: when you're ready to return, increase distance or intensity by no more than about 10% per week. Even once the pain is fully gone, jumping straight back to your old pace skips the readaptation period the tissue needs, and that's exactly what invites a relapse.

The bottom line: if the pain is spread out and eases with rest, treat it as shin splints and adjust your training load. If it's a sharp, single point that doesn't improve with rest, don't guess — see a doctor with a possible stress fracture in mind.
